summary: Discovery call to evaluate Redwood Dedicated reserved GPU capacity. ACME is considering moving inference off hosted endpoints to a Dedicated deployment due to data isolation and predictable latency. Main concerns: burst handling, autoscaling policies, cost tradeoffs vs hosted, private deployment/network constraints, and SOC2/KMS. Next steps: pricing, benchmarks, SE deep dive and security docs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-05-07 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (AE, Redwood); Maya Patel (SE, Redwood); Luis Gomez (Solutions Engineer, Redwood) -- Alex Chen (CTO, ACME); Priya Rao (Lead ML Eng, ACME); Samir Patel (Infra Lead, ACME); Tara Nguyen (Security, ACME)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we appreciate you taking the time. quick intro from my side Jordan Lee, i'm the AE on the account, with me is maya our se, and luis from solutions.
[00:10] Alex: hey thanks, Alex here. we wanted to run through dedicated options — isolation and predictable latency are the big drivers.
[00:20] Maya: great, do you want to kick off with a little context on what you're running today and the pain points?
[00:25] Priya: sure, yeah so brief context — we have an internal LLM infra powering search and summarization, currently on a mix of open-source models hosted on cloud vms and some hosted APIs from other providers. production sees peaks during business hours — roughly 600 qps aggregate across endpoints, but we see spikes that go to about 1.8k qps during campaigns. latency targets are 150-200ms p99 for short chat-style prompts, cost is material — we want better predictability and isolation for sensitive customer data.
[01:10] Samir: and on infra side we need dedicated GPU pools, we tried autoscaling groups but warmup time kills the latency when traffic bursts. so that's why reserved GPUs and faster burst capacity are interesting.
[01:25] Luis: thanks, that helps. quick clarifying q — is data residency or managed-private deployment a hard requirement or just preferred?
[01:35] Tara: Right now preference would be private/VPC with keys managed via our KMS, we also need audit logs, SSO/SAML, and SOC2 type evidence. if private isn't possible we'll need strict contractual controls.
[01:50] Jordan: understood. high-level our dedicated offering gives you reserved GPU capacity in your region with VPC peering and private networking options — you can either do Redwood-managed private (we host in a customer VPC) or an on-prem package in special cases. we support KMS integrations and audit logs.
[02:10] Alex: can you explain the burst strategy — say we commit to 16 GPUs but need to handle sudden 3x spikes for a few minutes, how does that work and what are the cost implications?
[02:20] Maya: sure. there are two levers — burst pools and autoscaling. you can reserve a baseline and allow burst to shared capacity or on-demand capacity if available. for Dedicated we offer configurable burst policies: short warm bursts (seconds) are possible using pre-warmed workers and KV cache priming, and for larger sustained bursts we recommend a hybrid of reserved + scheduled bursts or short-term capacity reservations.
[02:50] Priya: curious on the pre-warmed worker idea — what's the typical warmup and memory cost?
[02:55] Maya: depends on model size and quantization; for a 70B model in quantized int8 you might have warmup under 20s for the runtime to have KV cache ready, but cold start for very large models could be longer. part of what we do is kernel selection and pre-loading to reduce cold latency. (note: numbers approximate)
[03:15] Alex: ok.. but we've seen warmup take several minutes in our tests. does Redwood maintain a pool of hot workers that you can keep idle but ready?
[03:22] Maya: yes, you can configure a hot pool — those do incur the reserved capacity costs, but you can size them to cover typical spike magnitude. for unpredictable spikes we recommend a small hot pool plus burst routing to compatible smaller model variants (e.g., 70B -> 13B quantized) for graceful degradation.
[03:45] Samir: that routing idea is interesting — how seamless is it? does it require app changes?
[03:50] Luis: we expose routing policies in the deployment config — you can set latency SLO targets and a cost tier; the platform will route to fallback model variants automatically when the preferred capacity isn't available. you can also control it per-route. usually we surface it as a header in the response so the app can opt into toggling features if the model variant differs.
[04:10] Priya: do you support batch inference or continuous batching for embeddings? our workload is mixed — some low-latency chat, some large batched reranks.
[04:18] Maya: yes, the runtime supports continuous batching and configurable batch windows; you can tune per-route. embeddings/reranks tend to be cost-optimized with larger batch sizes, chat routes keep smaller windows.
[04:28] Alex: SLA wise what can we expect for Dedicated?
[04:30] Jordan: our Dedicated plan includes SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; we can share the SLA doc. typical 99.9% availability for the serving fabric, with escalation and runbook access.
[04:40] Tara: on the security front, KMS — do you integrate with our AWS KMS/HSM?
[04:44] Maya: yes we support AWS KMS and customer-managed keys for the Private control plane. for hosted Dedicated we can do envelope encryption with your KMS. for on-prem we can use local HSM integrations.
[04:56] Alex: pricing — how do you price reserved vs burst? is there a per-GPU per-hour charge plus overage?
[05:02] Jordan: pricing has two components: committed monthly reservation for GPUs (flat monthly fee per-GPU) which gives predictable capacity and better unit pricing; then burst/overage can be charged at an on-demand rate. we also offer short-term burst credits for initial ramp. we'll send a detailed worksheet with example numbers for your sizing.
[05:22] Priya: what's the contract minimum for Dedicated? we want to understand commitment lengths.
[05:26] Jordan: typical commitments are monthly or annual; we can do quarter pilots with month-to-month for the pilot, and annual for production for discounts.
[05:34] Samir: network setup: can you do VPC peering or AWS Transit? we have strict egress firewall rules and we need to keep traffic internal.
[05:41] Luis: we support VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink in many regions, and dedicated interconnects for on-prem. we'll need to coordinate network IP ranges and firewall rules; our SE will work with your infra to map ports and NAT rules.
[05:55] Tara: audit logs — do you provide token-level tracing? we need audit trails for PII access.
[06:00] Maya: yes, we provide request-level logs, token-level cost attribution, and audit events that can be forwarded to your SIEM. retention and redaction policies are configurable.
[06:12] Alex: can you talk about model lifecycle — pinning versions, rollouts, and evictions? we need a safe rollback capability if quality regresses after a model update.
[06:20] Maya: absolutely — the console supports version pinning, canary rollouts, and automatic rollback policies. you can tie regressions to eval sets and have automatic alerts. for Dedicated we can freeze model versions per-deployment and replicate the exact runtime environment.
[06:36] Priya: on quantization — do you recommend int8 or 4-bit for cost savings, and do you support per-model quantization profiles?
[06:44] Luis: yes, we have validated int8 and mixed 4-bit quant profiles depending on model and workload. we recommend running a small eval to measure quality delta; our Optimize tooling will propose quantization profiles per workload.
[06:58] Alex: a practical question — if we start with 16 GPUs reserved, and we want to scale to 64 over three months, how do we handle capacity ramping?
[07:08] Maya: you can update reservation sizes via API or console. there is lead time for provisioning GPUs in specific regions; we usually recommend planning for 2-4 week ramp windows for large capacity increases, or we can provision interim on-demand capacity to bridge. we'll include region-specific provisioning timelines in the worksheet.
[07:25] Priya: we also need to run performance tests against our real traffic. can we run a benchmark with our payloads and sample telemetry?
[07:31] Jordan: yes — next step would be to schedule a benchmark. maya/luis can run a SE-led performance run; we'll need sample payloads, distribution of prompt sizes and expected p99 latency targets.
[07:42] Alex: what's the support model during a pilot? we want SE on-call for the first week of pilot testing.
[07:47] Jordan: we can provide SE support and a runbook; for pilots we typically assign a solutions engineer for triage and the platform team for on-call. we can include that in the statement of work.
[07:56] Tara: one last security question — do you do customer-managed logging so logs never land in Redwood-managed buckets?
[08:02] Maya: yes, for Private deployments you can have all logs forwarded to your S3 or SIEM and not stored in Redwood buckets; for hosted Dedicated we can set up log forwarding and retention policies that meet compliance.
[08:13] Alex: ok sounds good. any sticky technical risks we should watch for?
[08:18] Luis: the main risks are cold start for very large models, network egress policies adding latency if peering isn't configured, and unexpected tokenization/quality regressions when using aggressive quantization. we mitigate with hot pools, KV caching, and eval runs before production rollouts.
[08:35] Priya: can you give a ballpark cost delta vs hosted? we want to know if Dedicated ultimately saves money at scale.
[08:41] Jordan: ballpark: if you're primarily long-lived steady-state traffic with predictable high qps, Dedicated often reduces unit cost by 20-40% depending on model and utilization; if your traffic is highly spiky and low average utilization, hosted can be cheaper. we'll model your numbers in the worksheet.
[08:58] Alex: competitor question — any notable differences vs Anthropic or AWS offering?
[09:02] Jordan: quick take: Anthropic/others are strong on model + API; Redwood focuses on serving economics and unified tooling across hosted/dedicated/private with opinionated routing, cache layers, and cost controls. vs AWS, we provide more high-level ML-serving optimizations out of the box and faster onboarding for model rollouts. but we compete and sometimes complement depending on customer needs.
[09:25] Tara: ok good. next steps recap?
[09:28] Jordan: recap: we'll send dedicated pricing + capacity worksheet (Jordan), maya will share benchmark templates and recommended model/quant profiles (Maya), schedule SE-led performance test (Jordan/Maya propose date), and attach SOC2 + security docs (Jordan). Alex to share sample telemetry and peak qps distribution. Samir to confirm VPC peering constraints.
[09:48] Alex: sounds good, propose the deep dive on 5/14.
[09:52] Maya: we'll block the SE time and follow up with a calendar invite and a runbook checklist.
[09:58] Priya: quick note — during the performance test we want to exercise both chat and embedding routes to see mixed workload behavior.
[10:05] Luis: noted. we'll include mixed workload scenario in the benchmark.
[10:10] Jordan: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the attachments and the worksheet.
[10:15] Alex: thanks, appreciate it.
